story:
Ruby ran to the gate at school pickup. Her tummy made a little growl. She saw her grandma waiting with a bright yellow bag.

"Can I have cookies now?" Ruby asked. Grandma shook her head. "Not yet. First we eat breakfast."

Ruby stopped. "What is breakfast?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "Breakfast is the first meal of the day."

They walked home. The sun felt warm on Ruby's face. Grandma's shoelace came untied, so they had to wait while she tied the string into a bow.

At home, Grandma said Ruby could help. Ruby looked in the cupboard. She saw cookies on the top shelf. "Those come later," said Grandma. Ruby saw oats in a big jar. She picked the jar up with both hands.

Grandma cooked the oats on the stove. Ruby stood far away and watched. The oats went pop, pop, pop. They smelled sweet like warm honey.

Ruby ate her bowl of oats all up. Her tummy felt happy and full. Then it was time for the rest of the day. Grandma helped her get dressed in a red shirt and blue pants.

"Can I have a cookie now?" Ruby asked. Grandma laughed and put one cookie in her hand. Ruby took a big bite. It was soft and sweet.

"This is the best cookie," said Ruby. Grandma wiped oat milk from Ruby's chin with a warm cloth. "That is because your tummy is full," said Grandma. Ruby held the cookie up to the window, and the light shone through the little hole in the middle.

story:
Elizabeth sat at the dinner table. She wanted the apple pie. It sat on the counter, far away.

"Can I have pie now?" she asked.

"Not now," said her dad. "We eat pie soon."

Elizabeth frowned. "Soon is a long time," she said.

"Soon means in a little while," said her dad.

Elizabeth took one bite of her chicken. She took another bite. She drank some milk. She looked at the pie again. It was still there.

"Now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said her dad. "Eat a little more."

Elizabeth ate her carrots, one by one. She waited some more. Then her dad stood up. He cut the pie. He put a big piece on her plate.

Elizabeth looked at her plate. The waiting was done. The pie was here now.

"Yesterday I had bread," she said. "Today I have pie. Tomorrow I can have pie again?"

"Maybe tomorrow," said her dad, smiling.

Elizabeth took her fork and played a little game. She made her pie into a moon shape. Then she ate it all up.

"Now pie is all gone," she said.

Her dad laughed. "And tomorrow," he said, "we can bake a new one together."

Emile looked out the window. Snow was falling on the backyard. "No school today," said his dad. "A snow day!"

Emile put on his boots. He put on his big coat. Then he walked into the snow. His boots made marks. Each step left a shape in the snow. Step, step, step.

Then Emile saw more marks. They were not his marks. They looked like little feet. "Look, Dad!" said Emile. "Little feet walked here!"

The little footprints went across the yard. Emile followed them. Step by step, he walked. The footprints went past the swing. They went under the big tree. They stopped at the fence.

The footprints led to a small door in the fence. It was the neighbour's door. Emile heard a sound. "Neigh!" A huge white horse stood there!

"Hello, horse," said Emile. The horse was gentle. It did not hurt Emile at all. The neighbour came out. "She escaped this morning," she said. "But her feet left footprints in the fresh snow."

Emile looked back at his own footprints. His feet made marks too. "My feet made footprints, Dad!" said Emile. Dad smiled. "You found the horse all by yourself."

Emile patted the horse's soft nose. "Good feet," he said. "Good footprints."

Her dad let her have one. Eva bit it. "Yum!" she said. It tasted big and sweet in her mouth.

She tried it again with a second strawberry. She held her nose. Plain again. She let go. Sweet again.

Her dad peeked over her shoulder. "What are you doing?" he asked.

Eva held up her strawberry. "My nose helps it taste big," she said.

Then her little bike bell rang in the hall. Ding, ding! Eva had not touched it. It was the cat, batting the bell with her paw.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Jasmine found a big cardboard box in the backyard. She wanted to play with it right away. Her friend Mya came over to play too.

"A car!" said Jasmine. She sat in the box and turned a pretend wheel. "Beep, beep!"

"A boat!" said Mya. She wanted the box to be a boat. "Row, row!"

They both wanted the box. Mya frowned. Jasmine frowned too. Then Mya had an idea.

"Let's take turns," said Mya. "First a car. Then a boat."

Jasmine smiled. She drove the box car around the grass. "Vroom!" The wheels were loud in her head. Then she climbed out and gave the box to Mya.

Mya rowed the box boat across the grass. "Splash, splash!"

Jasmine got her teddy bear. The bear needed a house. "The box can be a house now," she said. She put the bear inside and patted its head. Mya added a leaf for a blanket so the bear could dry off after the pretend bath.

"Time for bed, little bear," said Jasmine softly.

Then the girls climbed in together. The box was a house for everyone.

Ms. Holloway peeked over the fence and waved. "What a fine house," she called.

Jasmine waved back. "Come to our house!" she said.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Eli went to the park with his mom. It was a big festival day. There were flags and drums and lots of people. There were food stalls too.

Eli saw a food stall with sweet bread. He let go of his mom's hand. He walked toward the smell. The crowd was big. People walked in front of him. He could not see his mom. His tummy felt dizzy with worry.

Then Eli remembered. At a big crowded celebration, children stay close to their grown-up. He stood still and looked around. His mom was not far away. She was waving at him. He ran back and held her hand tight.

"Stay close now," his mom said. "The crowd is too big for little feet." They walked to the sweet bread stall together. His mom bought one piece. Eli took a bite. It was soft and warm. A little crumb fell, and a cloud of birds flew down to peck at it. Eli laughed and licked his sticky fingers. He held his mom's hand all the way home.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Dylan was in his bedroom. Maxime was coming to play today. Dylan felt so excited. His tummy was bouncy like a frog.

"I want to jump!" said Dylan. He jumped on the rug. He bounced on his bed. He shouted, "Maxime is coming!" He was so loud. His teddy fell over. Teddy looked angry about the big noise.

Dylan stopped. He sat down on the rug. He took a big, slow breath. He gave teddy a hug. "Waiting is hard," he said softly. He patted his bouncing legs, one pat, two pats. The frog in his tummy got small and still.

Then the door went ding-dong. Dylan walked slowly, slow like a snail. He opened the door. "Maxime!" said Dylan. "Come see my bedroom!" Maxime ran in, and they both laughed.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Thomas ran into the yard. The grass was wet and cold on his toes. Then he saw it. A small grey feather lay by the big tree.

"Look, Mommy, look!" he called. He picked it up. It was soft like his cat's tail. He petted it with one finger.

"Birds are animals that have feathers," said Mommy. "So a bird lost this one."

Thomas looked up. He looked at the tree. He looked at the roof. "Bird!" he shouted. A fat bird sat on the fence. It had grey feathers, all over!

The bird flew down. It hop, hop, hopped. It found a crumb. Then it flew away. Thomas waved.

"Come back!" he called. He held the feather up high. He was proud of it.

Inside, Mommy gave him toast and apple slices. Thomas ate his food. He put the feather on the window sill.

"Maybe the bird will see it," said Thomas. He watched and watched the yard. The toast was warm and good. Then he saw something move outside.

A bird was back on the fence. "It came back!" Thomas shouted. He ran to the window and tapped the glass, very soft. "Hi, bird. Hi!"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Harper sat on the big rug in the living room. Theo and Oceanne sat next to her. On the TV, a big game was on. Lots of people were running with a ball.

"Which team is mine?" Harper asked. She pointed at the TV. "They all look the same to me!"

Theo laughed. "They do not look the same. That team is red. That team is blue."

Harper looked hard. She saw one group in red shirts. She saw one group in blue shirts. "Oh! Red team and blue team!"

"Each team wears its own colors," said Mr. Kaur from the couch. "So you can tell the two teams apart."

The red team ran fast. A red player kicked the ball. It went into the net. "Goal!" everyone shouted. Harper jumped up and down.

Then the weather outside turned rainy. Rain tapped on the window. But inside, the game went on.

"Now I can help," Harper said. She clapped for the red team. "Go red! Go red!"

The blue team got the ball. "Oh no," said Oceanne. "I like blue."

"That is okay," said Theo. "You pick blue. I pick red."

Harper made a kind offer. "You can share my team too, Oceanne."

Oceanne giggled. "No thank you. Blue is mine."

The game went on and on. Harper watched the red shirts run. She watched the blue shirts run. She never mixed them up again.

Mr. Kaur passed out cups of juice. Harper took a big sip. On the TV, the red team kicked the ball again.

"Here it comes!" Harper shouted. "Watch the red one!"

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Brielle sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump down the road. She could see the pizza shop near the corner. "Pizza," said Brielle. "Yes," said her dad. "We will get pizza soon."

Brielle was thirsty. There was a juice box in the bag by her feet. "Give me juice!" she said. Her dad did not pass it to her. He kept both hands on the wheel. "Try again," he said. Brielle thought for a moment. "Juice, please," she said. Her dad smiled in the mirror. Then he reached back at the red light and gave her the juice box.

Brielle drank her juice. It did not hurt her tummy. It felt good and cold. "Thank you," she said. "You are welcome," said her dad.

At the pizza shop, the man gave Brielle one warm slice. "Please may I have more?" she asked. The man laughed and gave her a second slice. Brielle took a big bite. "Yum," she said. "More, please!"

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
It was bedtime. Jackson brushed his teeth in the bathroom. Then he ran to his room.

Jackson had a plan. He took out his crayons. He wanted to write a note for his dad. Jackson loved the playground, so he wrote, "LETSGOTHEPLAYGROUND." He put the paper under his pillow. His tummy felt happy and jumpy.

Dad came in to tuck him in. Jackson held up the note. "Read it, Dad!" Dad looked and looked. He turned the paper sideways. "Hmm. I cannot read this yet." Jackson's face went sad.

Dad picked up Jackson's bedtime book. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. He pointed at the page. "See the words? There is a space between one word and the next." Jackson leaned in close. He saw the little gaps. The words sat apart, like friends on a bench.

Jackson took his crayon. He drew little gaps in his note. Now it said, "LETS GO THE PLAYGROUND." Dad read it out loud. "Let's go the playground! Yes, tomorrow we can go." Jackson laughed and clapped. Dad kissed his head. "Sleep now, my writer."

Jackson hugged the note to his chest. "Goodnight, words," he whispered.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Elijah stood at the train station. He held a big red sign. It said GRANDMA in wobbly letters. It was hard to write letters that big.

The train rolled in. It was long and shiny. The doors went whoosh. People walked out one by one.

Then Elijah saw her. "Grandma!" he shouted. Grandma hugged him tight. Her coat smelled like flowers.

"Grandma, you are staying at my house for a whole week," said Elijah. "Are you my friend Andie's grandma too?"

Grandma laughed. "No, sweet pea. I am your mommy's mom."

Elijah blinked. "My mommy has a mom?"

"She does," said Grandma. "I am her mommy, just like your mommy is your mommy."

Mommy came over with the car keys. "Hi, Mom!" she said, and hugged Grandma too.

Elijah looked at Mommy. Then he looked at Grandma. Mommy's mom. Grandma was Mommy's mommy!

On the walk to the car, Elijah held Grandma's hand. "Grandma," he said, "when we get home, can we have warm milk?"

"We can have warm milk," said Grandma. "Your mommy can heat it. She learned that from me."

At home, Mommy heated the milk. Elijah held his cup with two hands. It was warm and sweet.

"Grandma," he said, "tomorrow can you read me a book? The train book?"

Grandma sat down beside him. "Every day for a whole week," she said.

Elijah snuggled close. The book had a shiny train on the cover. "That train looks just like your train," he said.

"It does," said Grandma. She opened the book to page one.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Leo sat on the big red couch at Mr. Wu's house. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Leo's friend Willa sat next to him with her milk.

"Who is winning?" asked Leo.

"I forgot," said Willa. She spun her cup and got a little dizzy. "Maybe the blue team. Or the red team!"

Mr. Wu laughed. "Look up there," he said. He pointed at the TV. "That is the scoreboard."

Leo looked. The scoreboard had two big numbers on it. One number was for each team. The blue team had the bigger number.

"The blue team is winning!" said Leo. He clapped his hands.

The red team kicked the ball into the net. The scoreboard changed. Now the numbers were the same.

"It's a tie!" said Willa.

"Look at that," said Leo. "The scoreboard always knows. I never have to remember!"

Leo dreamed of the day he would play in a big game too. But for now, he sipped his milk and watched the numbers go up and up.

"Willa, check the scoreboard," he said. "Quick, quick!"

The blue team scored again. Leo jumped up and did a happy dance.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Athena ran to the scooter. Gurasees was already on it. Athena grabbed the handle. "My turn!" she said. Gurasees held on tight.

Mr. Gagnon came over. He had a little sand timer. "When the sand runs out, the turn is over," he said. He turned it over. The sand began to fall. Gurasees rode in a circle. Athena watched the sand. It went down, down, down. The sand ran out. Gurasees stopped. "Your turn now," he said.

Athena got on the scooter. She rode to the fence and back. She peeked at the timer. The sand was almost gone. Athena stopped all by herself. "Sand is done!" she said. Gurasees laughed and took his turn.

Then Athena and Gurasees built a big sand hill together. They dug with their hands. Athena said, "I am hungry." Mr. Gagnon smiled. "Snack time," he said. "First, brush the sand off." Athena brushed off her hands. Then she sat with Gurasees and ate crackers, side by side in the sun.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Ethan went to the store with his dad. It was snowy outside. The store had a big shelf of books. Ethan wanted a book about a red lamp.

He found one. He sat down to read it. He opened the back page first. He ran his finger from right to left. The words felt mixed up. "Dad, the story is broken," he said.

His dad sat close beside him. "Turn to the front cover first," he said. Ethan turned the book around. He put his finger at the left side of the page. Then he slid it to the right. The words went in a row, one after another. It sounded like a real story.

A girl named Maksim from his class peeked over. "That is my favorite book," she said. Ethan smiled and read on. His finger moved across the page, left to right, all the way to the end.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Brooklyn had a cold. Her nose was stuffy and runny. She sat on the couch with a soft blanket. Her tummy made a little rumble. "I want a snack," she said.

Her mom put crackers and apple slices on a plate. Brooklyn took a tissue. She blew her nose. It made a big honking sound. Then she reached for a cracker.

"Wait," her mom said. "Your hands need soap and water first." Brooklyn felt a bit sad about waiting. But she slid down from the couch. She went to the sink. She pumped the soap. She rubbed her hands under the water. Bubbles grew between her fingers. "I will tell my teddy," she said. "He should wash his paws too."

Then Brooklyn sat back down. She picked up a cracker with clean hands. She crunched it. The apple was sweet and juicy. Her mom smiled and tucked the blanket around her. Brooklyn gave one apple slice to her teddy, and pretended he took a big bite.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Everly had a sparkly pink dress. She wore it all day at Katelyn's party. She twirled. She jumped. She ate cake until her tummy was full.

Now it was dark. Everly did not want to take off her dress. "I want to sleep in my dress," she said. Her dad helped her change anyway. He put on her soft pajamas. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in," he said.

Everly got into bed. The pajamas felt warm and cozy. Her dress had been scratchy. The pajamas were soft like a blanket. She snuggled down and felt safe. Her dad tucked her in.

"Night night," he said.

Everly closed her eyes. "Night night, dress," she whispered. "You can come out tomorrow."

And soon she fell fast asleep.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Milo sat at the little table in the backyard. He had a big paper pumpkin to paint. He looked in the paint box. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. But there was no orange paint. "Where is the orange?" he wondered.

His friend Hayes came over. Hayes held up the red jar. "Want to paint it red?" asked Hayes. Milo shook his head. He wanted a real orange pumpkin. Then he had an idea. What if the paints could mix?

Milo put a dot of red on his brush. Then he put a dot of yellow next to it. He picked up the brush and swirled them together. Round and round they went. The red spread into the yellow. The yellow spread into the red. Then something new appeared. Orange! Bright, orange paint!

Milo dipped his brush in the orange. He painted the pumpkin. He painted the stem green. He touched the wet paint with one finger. It felt a little slimy. He laughed and wiped it on the paper. "Look, Hayes! Red and yellow made orange!" said Milo. Hayes grabbed a brush too. "My turn to mix!"
